To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the overall sequence diversity is 3.81 x 10(-3) and that intragenic LD is very high, although not uniformly distributed across the gene.

(i) intragenic LD is generally very strong, (ii) the frequency of low-frequency alleles and non-synonymous coding variants is higher in negative LD, and (iii) gene-specific LD patterns make it difficult to provide universal guidelines for selecting useful polymorphisms.

the extent of LD in candidate genes for common diseases is heterogeneous, and that, for most genes, the power to detect association between a functional polymorphism and a disease phenotype is likely to be low".
In summary, our research is concerned with
the characterization of genetic variation in candidate genes for complex diseases.
the development of methods for identifying the most useful polymorphic markers in association studies and with the development of a new generation of association studies.
the development of new approaches to identify the genetic basis of complex traits and to improve our understanding of the mechanisms of common human diseases.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no single best approach to the design of association studies.
the more information we have, the more we realize that we still do not have enough information.
the power of genetic association studies is likely to depend on the specific characteristics of each gene, which are difficult to predict.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
LD in candidate genes is highly variable, with many polymorphisms in negative LD and with a large fraction of the pairs of polymorphims exhibiting complete LD.
the genetic architecture of complex diseases is more complex than previously anticipated.

, in the absence of functional information, the choice of the best markers for association studies of complex diseases is not straightforward and that the most useful polymorphism is likely to be different in different populations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the choice of the most useful markers for association studies should not be based solely on the LD between polymorphisms, but also on their functional relevance.
association studies should concentrate not only on the overall sequence diversity of candidate genes, but also on the overall sequence variability of functionally important intergenic regions.
the choice of polymorphisms to be studied in association studies is critical and should be based on the overall variability of the region of interest.
